youtube.aciklama:
How do you read a systematic review and meta-analysis? In this lesson we learn how to build a clinical question with PICO, levels of evidence, the steps of a systematic review and the PRISMA flow diagram, risk of bias, meta-analysis, the forest plot, heterogeneity, certainty of evidence with GRADE, and how to use clinical guidelines.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Higgins JPT et al. (eds.) Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions; Page MJ et al. The PRISMA 2020 statement. BMJ (2021); Guyatt GH et al. GRADE: an emerging consensus on rating quality of evidence and strength of recommendations. BMJ (2008); OCEBM Levels of Evidence Working Group, The Oxford 2011 Levels of Evidence; NICE, Hearing loss in adults: assessment and management (NG98, 2018); Joint Committee on Infant Hearing, Year 2019 Position Statement.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: PICO, levels of evidence, forest plot, guidelines
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will recall how to build a clinical question with PICO and learn how a systematic review is done.
Step by step, we will read meta-analyses, forest plots, the certainty of evidence and clinical guidelines.
In the lesson on reading scientific articles, we saw the PICO format for structuring a clinical question.
In this lesson, let the patients in our example question be adults with mild to moderate hearing loss.
The intervention is hearing aid use.
The comparison is no hearing aid, or being on a waiting list.
The outcome is the change in score on a hearing-related quality of life scale.
Besides treatment, questions can concern diagnosis, screening and prognosis; each type of question has a different best study design.
In the Oxford levels, the top level for treatment questions is a systematic review of randomized trials.

cumleler.yazi: It is followed by a single randomized controlled trial, or RCT.
cumleler.ses: It is followed by a single randomized controlled trial, or R C T.

cumleler: Next come cohort or follow-up studies without random allocation.
Case series and case-control studies are at lower levels.
At the bottom is reasoning from physiology.
But the level is only a starting point: a poorly done review also misleads, so we will learn to read how it was done.
In a traditional narrative review, the author summarizes studies they know or select; the selection is often not transparent.
A systematic review, by contrast, starts with a protocol written in advance and often entered in a registry.
A comprehensive search is run in several databases with keywords set in advance.
Which studies will be included or excluded is defined in advance with explicit criteria.
The quality of each included study, or its risk of bias, is assessed with standard tools.
These steps let another researcher repeat the same review; transparency is the essence of a systematic review.
The process starts with a protocol that contains the PICO question and the inclusion criteria.
The search is not limited to PubMed; other databases, clinical trial registries and unpublished studies are also searched.
Titles, abstracts and full texts are screened independently by two reviewers; disagreements are resolved by discussion.
Participant numbers, intervention and outcome data are extracted from each study with a standard form.
The last step is synthesis: if studies are similar enough they are combined numerically; if not, results are summarized in narrative form.

cumleler.yazi: A checklist called PRISMA is used to report these steps; it was updated in 2020.
cumleler.ses: A checklist called PRISMA is used to report these steps; it was updated in twenty twenty.

cumleler: Every systematic review has a flow diagram showing how studies were filtered out; the numbers here are only examples.
First, records found in all databases are pooled, and duplicates that appear in more than one place are removed.
In title and abstract screening, studies unrelated to the question are excluded.
The full texts of the remaining studies are read, and each exclusion is recorded with its reason.
Finally, the number of studies included in the review, and in any meta-analysis, is stated.
As a reader, this diagram lets you see how thorough the search was and what was excluded and why.
In selection bias, how groups are formed affects the result; we ask whether random allocation was done correctly and concealed.
If participants or assessors know the group, subjective outcomes such as questionnaires may be affected; this is a blinding problem.
If more participants drop out of one group, the result can be misleading.
Reporting only significant outcomes instead of those promised in the protocol is selective reporting.
Studies with negative results being published less often is called publication bias; it can shift the whole result of a review.
Standard tools such as the Cochrane risk of bias tool rate these domains as low, unclear or high risk for each study.
Meta-analysis statistically combines the results of several studies to get a single pooled estimate.
Results are expressed with a common effect measure: for example, mean difference for continuous outcomes and risk ratio for binary ones.
Each study gets a weight; large studies with precise estimates contribute more to the result.
A fixed effect model assumes one true effect, while a random effects model allows for real differences between studies.
A meta-analysis is only as good as the studies it combines; pooling weak studies can produce a precise but wrong result.
So the result of a meta-analysis must be read together with the risk of bias and the consistency between studies.
The result of a meta-analysis is shown with a forest plot; the plot on screen is a teaching example.
Each row is a study: the dot shows that study's estimate, and the horizontal line its ninety five percent confidence interval.
The vertical line in the middle is the line of no effect; for a mean difference, this value is zero.
Study C's confidence interval crosses the zero line, so this study alone showed no significant difference.
Studies with narrow intervals are more precise and get more weight in the meta-analysis; most plots show this with a larger square.
The diamond at the bottom is the pooled estimate: its center shows the overall effect, and its two ends the confidence interval.
In this example the diamond does not cross zero and lies fully in favor of the device, so the pooled evidence suggests a benefit.
Finally, whether this difference is clinically meaningful is judged against the minimal important difference from the statistics lesson.
Heterogeneity means results differ more than chance can explain; first, check on the plot whether the intervals overlap.

cumleler.yazi: As a numerical measure, the I² statistic is given; it shows, as a percentage, how much of the variation comes from real differences.
cumleler.ses: As a numerical measure, the I squared statistic is given; it shows, as a percentage, how much of the variation comes from real differences.

cumleler.yazi: According to the Cochrane Handbook, an I² below forty percent may often be unimportant; these limits are a rough guide.
cumleler.ses: According to the Cochrane Handbook, an I squared below forty percent may often be unimportant; these limits are a rough guide.

cumleler.yazi: An I² above seventy five percent is read as very high heterogeneity and calls a single pooled result into question.
cumleler.ses: An I squared above seventy five percent is read as very high heterogeneity and calls a single pooled result into question.

cumleler: In audiology, different degrees of loss, different device technologies and different scales are common causes of heterogeneity.
A good review explores the cause of heterogeneity with subgroup analyses, and the reader looks for this in the discussion.

cumleler: The GRADE approach is widely used to rate how trustworthy the evidence is.
GRADE gives the certainty of evidence at four levels: high, moderate, low and very low.
Evidence from randomized trials starts high and is downgraded for bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias.
Indirectness means the patients or outcomes in the studies differ from your question; for example, studies only of people with severe loss.
Imprecision means a very wide confidence interval, so the true effect could be either important or trivial.
Checking this certainty level for each outcome in a review's summary table is one of the fastest and most valuable reading steps.
A clinical guideline is a document that offers practice recommendations based on systematic reviews.
A good guideline is prepared by a panel of different specialists and patient representatives.
Each recommendation is graded as strong or conditional, based on the certainty of evidence and the balance of benefit and harm.
The reader checks the guideline's methods, currency and the authors' conflict of interest statements; standard tools exist for this.

cumleler.yazi: The UK adult hearing loss guideline and the 2019 position statement of the Joint Committee on Infant Hearing are often cited examples.
cumleler.ses: The U K adult hearing loss guideline and the twenty nineteen position statement of the Joint Committee on Infant Hearing are often cited examples.

cumleler: A guideline prepared abroad is used after adapting it to the health system, regulations and patient needs in Türkiye.

sahneler.metin: In a systematic review, look first at the summary of findings table: effect size, confidence interval and certainty of evidence are given together for each outcome.
cumleler: A clinical tip: if you are short on time, go straight to the summary of findings table of the systematic review.
This table gives, for each outcome, the effect size, the confidence interval, the number of participants and the certainty of evidence.
Then check whether the included patients resemble your own patient.
These three pieces of information usually show how much the review should influence your clinical decision.

Certainty with GRADE, recommendations in guidelines

cumleler: A question built with PICO determines the search strategy and which evidence is suitable.
A systematic review differs from a narrative one by its protocol, thorough search, explicit criteria and risk of bias assessment.

cumleler.yazi: In a forest plot, each study appears as a dot with an interval and the pooled result as a diamond; heterogeneity is tracked with I².
cumleler.ses: In a forest plot, each study appears as a dot with an interval and the pooled result as a diamond; heterogeneity is tracked with I squared.

cumleler: GRADE rates the certainty of evidence at four levels; guidelines turn this evidence into recommendations adapted to local conditions.

sahneler.aciklama: If the pooled confidence interval includes the _no effect_ value, no significant difference has been shown.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: in a forest plot, the diamond showing the pooled estimate crosses the line of no effect. What does this mean?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: no statistically significant difference was shown in the pooled result.
This does not mean the effect is definitely absent either; the evidence may be insufficient, so look at how wide the interval is.
